newsitem.title: JAPAN: Electronics, car firms to lead Japan profit growth.
newsitem.headline: Electronics, car firms to lead Japan profit growth.

text.p: Corporate Japan's profit growth in the business year starting next April will likely be led by blue-chip firms in the electronics and automobile industries, research firms say.
But they expect overall growth to slow in comparison with the current business year.

"Electronics firms' earnings will be buoyed by improved profitability in the semiconductor business as well as strong demand from telecoms and computer-related businesses," Daiwa Research Institute said in a report.
Carmakers, meanwhile, will continue to enjoy robust sales both in the domestic and U.S. markets, others said.
Daiwa Research expects electronics and automobile firms' parent current profits in the 1997/98 business year to account for 44.7 percent of growth at the 547 major firms it surveys.
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities, such as investment in stocks.

The research unit of Daiwa Securities Co also said electronics firms will be more conspicuous in leading Japan Inc's 1997/98 profit growth than carmakers, who are making the biggest profits this business year.
The electronics sector will be helped by improved profitability from semiconductors and will also benefit from a rapidly growing mobile phone market in Japan.

Analysts said the arrival on the market of digital video discs (DVD) will also create new demand. The DVD looks like a compact disc but can hold much more data. Warner Home Video said on Monday it will start selling movies on DVDs in Japan this month.
Daiwa said the electronics sector's parent current profits would surge 13.9 percent in 1997/98, compared with a 2.1 percent rise forecast for 1996/97.
The automobile sector's profit growth is expected to decline from 80.7 percent this year to 12.8 percent.
The reports said overall corporate profit growth in 1997/98 will likely slow from the current year due mainly to the stabilising dollar-yen exchange rate.

Okasan Economic Research Institute said it expects parent current profits of 343 major firms quoted on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, excluding financial institutions, to grow 6.1 percent in the 1997/98 business year, down from a projected 9.9 percent growth forecast for the current business year to March 31.
"As the yen stabilises from a declining trend, Japan's major companies are no longer able to count on such windfalls to boost their earnings in fiscal 1997," said Okasan analyst Satoshi Toyonaga.
Okasan said the yen's value against the dollar will likely average 113 yen in the first half of 1997/98, down about five yen from a year earlier.
But the yen's decline was much more drastic in the first half of 1996/97, when it fell nearly 20 yen from the same period in the previous year.
Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics said Japanese companies' profits would rise 0.8 percentage point for each one yen decline in the yen against the dollar.
There is also some uncertainty clouding corporate earnings for the next business year, analysts said.

"The proposed rise in the consumption tax, which is under deliberation in parliament, could discourage consumers and as a result hurt retailers," said Yuichi Matsushita, a senior strategist at Nikko Research Center.
